### Per-school decomposition {#sec-final-school-model}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal" title="Nerdy details"}

```{r}
#| label: per-school-setup
#| include: false
# School estimates and groups were prepared by the fitting setup.
per_100 <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f", 100 * x)
percent <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
estimated <- school_estimates$schools
national_2025 <- national_decomposition(decomposition, cvte_pupils) |>
    filter(test_year == school_year)
all_schools <- filter(school_groups, level == "national")$decomposition[[1]]
leniency_z <- estimated$delta / estimated$se_delta
model_eligible <- vapply(
    school_estimates$results, \(r) r$decomposition[["eligible"]], 0
)
```

To go from the Netherlands to single schools, we fit the model of @sec-measurement-model to each school $s$ separately.
The pupils of a school have their own distribution of the common factor, $\theta_p \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_s, \sigma^2_s)$,
and the teachers of the school have a leniency $\delta_s$ that shifts their provisional advice:

$$
L^*_p = \theta_p + \delta_s + \epsilon_{L, p}.
$$ {#eq-school-teacher}

A positive $\delta_s$ means that the teachers advise higher than the teacher of the national model ($\delta_s = 0$) for the same pupils,
and a negative $\delta_s$ that they advise lower.
The thresholds, the teacher error, and the parameters of the tests are the national ones of `{r} school_year` (@tbl-original-parameters).
DUO does not say whether a school took the paper or the digital version of IEP or Lib, so we use a mix of both versions, weighted by their national number of pupils.

For each school, DUO gives the number of pupils with a higher, equal, and lower test advice, the number of raised advices [@duo_heroverweging],
the final advice per category [@duo_advies], and the test [@duo_eindscores].
Counts below five are suppressed, and we use their midpoint 2.5.
We fit $(\mu_s, \sigma_s, \delta_s)$ to these counts by maximum likelihood,
where the final advice is the provisional advice, raised to the test result for the school's share of raised advices.
Most schools are small (median `{r} median(estimated$total)` pupils), so we use an empirical Bayes prior:
we first fit the schools with at least 50 pupils, and use the spread of their estimates as a normal prior for all schools,
so that the estimates of small schools move towards the average.
The final advice in the DUO data is somewhat higher than the model predicts from the provisional advice and the raises, which would make all schools look lenient.
We absorb this in a national offset of `{r} sprintf("%.2f", school_estimates$model$final_shift)` in the final advice,
so that the leniency of the schools is centred on the national teacher.

The decomposition of a school then follows @eq-shapley with four sources:
the teacher error, the teachers' leniency ($\delta_s$ instead of zero), the test error, and the test menu (the school's test instead of the reference test).
Groups of schools are averages of their schools, weighted by their number of pupils.
Over all `{r} format(nrow(estimated), big.mark = ",")` schools, the school-level model gives a category design of `{r} per_100(all_schools[["category_design"]])` in 100 pupils
and `{r} per_100(all_schools[["eligible"]])` eligible pupils in 100,
close to the national model (`{r} per_100(national_2025$category_design)` and `{r} per_100(national_2025$eligible)`).
For single schools, the model's share of eligible pupils correlates `{r} sprintf("%.2f", cor(model_eligible, estimated$higher / estimated$total))` with the observed share of pupils with a higher test advice.
The teachers of `{r} percent(mean(leniency_z <= -2))` of the schools are clearly stricter than the national teacher ($\delta_s$ at least two standard errors below zero),
and those of `{r} percent(mean(leniency_z >= 2))` are clearly more lenient.
:::
